title: Can Low Vitamin D Cause Weight Gain? What the Research Shows
summary: Can low vitamin D cause weight gain? Why body fat lowers vitamin D, what trials like VITAL found about supplements and weight, and which test shows a real deficiency.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


Low vitamin D has not been shown to cause weight gain. People with more body fat do tend to have lower vitamin D levels, but the best evidence suggests the body fat comes first: a large genetic study found that a higher BMI leads to lower vitamin D, while any effect of low vitamin D on BMI is likely small ([Vimaleswaran et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23393431/) ). Randomized trials found that vitamin D supplements neither help people lose weight nor make them gain it. A 25-hydroxyvitamin D blood test shows whether your level is actually low.


For the general signs of a low level, see[low vitamin D symptoms](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-vitamin-d) . For what the marker is and how it is measured, see the[vitamin D biomarker overview](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/vitamin-d) . This page answers one question: how vitamin D and body weight are connected, and what that means for testing and supplements.


## The short answer


- **Low vitamin D is not an established cause of weight gain.** Observational studies link lower vitamin D with higher body weight, but that kind of study cannot show which causes which ([Chou et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33513226/) ).
- **Body fat lowers measured vitamin D.** Vitamin D is fat-soluble, and in people with more body fat it is spread through a larger volume, so less of it shows up in the blood ([Drincic et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22262154/) ).
- **Supplements do not change weight.** In the VITAL trial, 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day for two years did not change weight, BMI, waist size or body fat compared with placebo ([Chou et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33513226/) ).
- **Supplements do not cause weight gain either.** The same trial found no weight change in either direction.
- **Testing is the way to know.** The 25-hydroxyvitamin D test, also called 25(OH)D, is the most accurate way to see if you have enough vitamin D ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) ).


## Can low vitamin D cause weight gain?


There is no good evidence that low vitamin D causes weight gain. The strongest test of the question comes from genetics. Some people carry gene variants that lower their vitamin D level for life, regardless of diet or body weight. If low vitamin D caused weight gain, those people should be heavier on average.


They are not. A Mendelian randomization study pooled 21 adult cohorts of up to 42,024 people and checked the result in a genetic consortium of 123,864 more. Gene variants that lower vitamin D were not associated with BMI. The authors concluded that any effect of lower vitamin D on BMI is likely small ([Vimaleswaran et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23393431/) ).


Ideas about how low vitamin D might promote fat gain, for example through appetite or fat cell signaling, remain unproven in people. The randomized trials below, which tested vitamin D directly, did not find an effect on weight.


## The reverse link: more body fat lowers vitamin D


The link that does hold up runs the other way. Carrying more body fat lowers the vitamin D level measured in the blood.


- **The genetic evidence points this way.** In the same Mendelian randomization study, each 1 kg/m² higher BMI was associated with 1.15% lower 25(OH)D. Gene variants that raise BMI also lowered vitamin D: a 10% higher genetically predicted BMI meant 4.2% lower 25(OH)D ([Vimaleswaran et al., 2013](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23393431/) ).
- **The pattern is gradual.** Among 16,515 older adults in VITAL, average 25(OH)D before treatment was 32.3 ng/mL at normal weight, 30.5 ng/mL with overweight, 29.0 ng/mL with class I obesity and 28.0 ng/mL with class II obesity, after adjusting for other factors ([Tobias et al., 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36648947/) ).
- **Losing weight tends to raise vitamin D.** In a 12-month trial of 439 postmenopausal women with overweight or obesity, those who lost 15% or more of their weight saw their 25(OH)D rise by 7.7 ng/mL on average, compared with 2.1 ng/mL in those who lost less than 5% ([Mason et al., 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21613554/) ). A systematic review found an increase in vitamin D status with weight loss in 18 of 23 trials ([Pannu et al., 2016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26923506/) ).


### Why body fat lowers the number: dilution and storage


Two explanations are discussed, and both may play a part.


- **Dilution.** In 686 unsupplemented adults, the drop in vitamin D with obesity was fully explained by vitamin D being spread through a larger body size. The study found no evidence that fat tissue traps vitamin D ([Drincic et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22262154/) ).
- **Storage in fat.** An earlier study gave people with and without obesity the same dose of ultraviolet light or oral vitamin D. After whole-body UV exposure, the rise in blood vitamin D3 was 57% lower in people with obesity, even though their skin made vitamin D normally. The authors attributed this to vitamin D being deposited in body fat ([Wortsman et al., 2000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10966885/) ).


A later review concluded that dilution explains much of the effect, with storage in fat and conversion to inactive forms also playing a role ([Pannu et al., 2016](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26923506/) ).


Either way, a low vitamin D result in someone with more body fat is real and worth knowing about. It just does not mean the low vitamin D caused the weight.


## Is it harder to lose weight with low vitamin D?


Trials have not shown that low vitamin D makes weight loss harder. Two trials in postmenopausal women with overweight or obesity tested this directly.


- In a 12-month diet and exercise trial, women’s baseline vitamin D status did not change how much weight or body fat they lost ([Mason et al., 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21613554/) ).
- In a second 12-month trial, 218 women aged 50 to 75 with 25(OH)D between 10 and 32 ng/mL followed a reduced-calorie diet and an exercise program. Half took 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day and half took placebo. Both groups lost similar weight, 7.1 kg with vitamin D and 7.4 kg with placebo, and waist size, body fat and trunk fat changed similarly ([Mason et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24622804/) ).


That second trial had one secondary finding. Women on vitamin D who reached 32 ng/mL or higher lost more weight than those who did not, 8.8 kg compared with 5.6 kg. Because this compares women by the level they reached rather than by random assignment, it cannot show that vitamin D caused the extra loss. Women who lose more weight also tend to see their vitamin D rise, as described above.


## Does taking vitamin D help with weight loss?


Vitamin D supplements have not been shown to help with weight loss.


- **VITAL.** In 771 adults (men 50 and older, women 55 and older), 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day for two years did not change weight, BMI, waist size, or fat and lean tissue measured by DXA scan, compared with placebo. Results did not differ by starting vitamin D level. The one exception was a slight improvement in body fat percentage in people who started at a normal BMI, not in those with overweight or obesity, and the authors called for more study of it ([Chou et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33513226/) ).
- **Meta-analysis.** A review of randomized trials that gave vitamin D without calorie restriction pooled 12 trials and found no effect on body weight, fat mass, body fat percentage or lean mass. The small drop in BMI it observed was not statistically significant ([Pathak et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24528624/) ).
- **With a diet program.** Adding vitamin D3 to a diet and exercise program did not increase weight loss in the 12-month trial above ([Mason et al., 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24622804/) ).


Correcting a real deficiency still matters for its own reasons. Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium and keeps muscles and bones working normally ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) ). For food, sunlight and supplement options, see[how to raise vitamin D levels naturally](https://mitohealth.com/guide/raising-vitamin-d-levels-naturally) and[how much vitamin D to take](https://mitohealth.com/blog/vitamin-d-supplements-how-much-should-you-really-take) .


### Body weight changes the response to supplements


People with more body fat get a smaller rise in vitamin D from the same dose. In VITAL, 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 a day raised 25(OH)D at every weight, but the increase was significantly smaller at higher BMI ([Tobias et al., 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36648947/) ). The dilution study concluded that vitamin D replacement needs to be adjusted for body size to reach a given blood level ([Drincic et al., 2012](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22262154/) ). The Endocrine Society’s 2011 guideline stated that adults with obesity need at least two to three times more vitamin D than others their age to treat and prevent deficiency ([Holick et al., 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21646368/) ). The 2024 guideline does not cover treating a diagnosed deficiency, so the right amount is a decision for your clinician, and a retest shows whether a supplement is working.


## Can taking vitamin D cause weight gain?


No trial has shown that vitamin D supplements cause weight gain. In VITAL, weight and BMI did not change with vitamin D3 compared with placebo over two years ([Chou et al., 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33513226/) ).


Too much vitamin D does cause problems, but weight gain is not among them. MedlinePlus lists nausea and vomiting, poor appetite, constipation, muscle weakness and weight loss as symptoms of too much vitamin D, which usually comes from supplements ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) ). See[high vitamin D symptoms](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-vitamin-d) for more.


## Other causes of weight gain worth testing


If you are gaining weight without a clear reason, some causes show up on blood tests. These are more direct explanations than low vitamin D.


- **An underactive thyroid.** MedlinePlus lists weight gain, fatigue or feeling slowed down, feeling cold, and constipation among the symptoms of hypothyroidism, and blood tests for TSH and free T4 are used to check for it ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000353.htm) ). Muscle aches and weakness appear on both the thyroid and the vitamin D symptom lists. See[thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/thyroid-stimulating-hormone) , or order a[TSH blood test](https://mitohealth.com/products/thyroid-stimulating-hormone-tsh) on its own.
- **High cortisol.** Cushing syndrome, from long-term high cortisol, typically causes weight gain around the trunk with thinner arms and legs, a round face and wide purple stretch marks ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000410.htm) ). See[how high cortisol can cause weight gain](https://mitohealth.com/blog/how-high-cortisol-can-cause-weight-gain-and-what-you-can-do-about-it) and the[cortisol overview](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/cortisol) .
- **Low iron.** Iron deficiency anemia can make you feel tired, cold and dizzy ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/anemia.html) ). That tiredness is easy to mistake for the fatigue people link with low vitamin D.[Ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/ferritin) shows your iron stores.
- **Hormone changes.** For how estrogen shifts around perimenopause and menopause relate to weight, see[does estrogen cause weight gain](https://mitohealth.com/blog/does-estrogen-cause-weight-gain) .


For how thyroid hormones relate to energy and weight more broadly, see[thyroid hormones, energy and weight](https://mitohealth.com/blog/thyroid-hormones-t4-tsh-energy-weight-health-longevity) .


## Which test to ask for and how to read it


Ask for a **25-hydroxyvitamin D** test, also written 25(OH)D or calcidiol. Your liver converts vitamin D into this form, and measuring it is the most accurate way to see if you have enough. Another test, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D or calcitriol, measures the active form. It is used for kidney problems and abnormal calcium, not to check vitamin D status ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) ).


### Who should test


The Endocrine Society’s 2024 guideline found no clinical trial evidence supporting routine 25(OH)D screening in the general population, including people with obesity or darker skin. It suggests against routine testing for people without an established reason to test ([Demay et al., 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38828931/) ). Weight on its own is therefore not a strong reason to test.


MedlinePlus lists situations where a test makes sense ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) ):


- symptoms such as bone pain, muscle weakness or aches, or fractures;
- low bone density or osteoporosis;
- weight loss surgery, or a condition that affects absorption such as Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis or celiac disease;
- kidney or liver disease;
- medicines that affect vitamin D levels, including steroids, certain statins and weight-loss medicines;
- checking whether a supplement is raising a low level, or whether a level is too high.


### How to read the result


Results are usually reported as total vitamin D, which is D2 and D3 added together. MedlinePlus describes four categories: deficient, insufficient, sufficient or optimal, and toxic or possible toxicity ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/vitamin-d-test/) ). The exact cutoffs vary by lab and by guideline.


Reference point What it means


At least 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) The Institute of Medicine found this level meets the bone health needs of at least 97.5% of people, and higher levels were not consistently linked with more benefit ([Ross et al., 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21118827/) )


Below 20 ng/mL, or 21 to 29 ng/mL The Endocrine Society’s 2011 guideline defined deficiency as below 20 ng/mL and insufficiency as 21 to 29 ng/mL ([Holick et al., 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21646368/) ). Its 2024 guideline found no clear evidence defining an optimal target for disease prevention ([Demay et al., 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38828931/) )


Lower than expected for your intake and body size More body fat lowers the measured level and blunts the rise from supplements ([Tobias et al., 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36648947/) )


If your result is low, the useful questions are why, and whether bones or muscles are affected. For what a low result means and how it is usually corrected, see[vitamin D deficiency symptoms and solutions](https://mitohealth.com/blog/vitamin-d-deficiency-symptoms-and-solutions) . For supplement forms, see[which vitamin D form to take](https://mitohealth.com/guide/which-vitamin-d-form) . For what the test costs at different labs, see the[vitamin D test cost guide](https://mitohealth.com/guide/vitamin-d-test-cost) .

## Frequently asked questions


### Can low vitamin D cause belly fat?


There is no good evidence that it does. People with more abdominal fat tend to have lower vitamin D levels, but in the VITAL trial, two years of daily vitamin D3 did not change waist size or body fat measured by DXA scan compared with placebo. The link is better explained by body fat lowering the blood level of vitamin D.


### Is it harder to lose weight with low vitamin D?


Trials have not shown that. In a 12-month diet and exercise program for women with low or borderline vitamin D, those given vitamin D3 lost about the same weight as those given placebo, and baseline vitamin D status did not change how much weight people lost in an earlier diet and exercise trial. Losing weight tends to raise the vitamin D level instead.


### Does taking vitamin D help with weight loss?


Not on its own. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found no effect of vitamin D on body weight or fat mass without calorie restriction, and the VITAL trial found no effect on weight or body composition over two years. Taking vitamin D can correct a deficiency, which matters for bone and muscle health.


### Does taking vitamin D make you gain weight?


No trial has shown that. Weight did not change with vitamin D3 compared with placebo in VITAL. Very high vitamin D levels from too much supplement are linked to poor appetite, nausea and weight loss rather than weight gain.


### How do you feel when vitamin D is extremely low?


Many people with low vitamin D notice nothing. When a deficiency is severe or lasts a long time, it can cause bone pain, muscle weakness or aches, and soft bones that break more easily, a condition called osteomalacia in adults. A blood test is the only way to know your level.


### Which test shows if vitamin D is low?


The 25-hydroxyvitamin D test, also written 25(OH)D or calcidiol. It is the most accurate way to check vitamin D status. The 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D test measures the active form and is used for kidney and calcium problems, not to check whether you have enough vitamin D.
